## Hypothesis 2

Analytic approaches for Hypothesis 2: "Higher status participants are more verbose
than are lower status participants." Extracted from the collected Hypothesis 1 file;
each block continues the same analyst's script, so the library calls and data import
sit at the top of that analyst's Hypothesis 1 block.


-Analyst 1
```{r}
my_data <- read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

# OK I do the second hypothesis now.
# "Higher status participants are more verbose than are lower status participants."
# I operationalize Verbose as number of characters in a text. At least for now.
# --------------------------------
my_data <- mutate(my_data, log_num_char=log(my_data$Number.Characters))
# --------------------------------
d <- dplyr::select(my_data, log_num_char, Academic, Female, PhD_Institution_US_Bin:PreviousCitations)
d <- d %>% mutate(factor_academic=as.factor(Academic), factor_female=as.factor(Female), factor_aca_hier=as.factor(AcademicHierarchyStrict))
# --------------------------------
reg2 <- lm(log_num_char~AcademicHierarchyStrict+Female+Academic, data=d)
summary(reg2) ##Reviewer 2 COMMENT: The reported effect size for Hyp 2 can be found here (-0.16150) which is the reg coef for AcademicHierarchyStrict
library(apaTables)
apa.reg.table(reg2) ##Reviewer 2 COMMENT: cannot find the model of reported effect sizes for Hyp 2
```

-Analyst 3
```{r}

#'##Data preparation
#'####Required R libraries
#rm(list = ls())
require(lme4)
require(piecewiseSEM)
require(influence.ME)

#'####Reading in the my_data
my_data <- read.csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

#'####Examining the my_data
#View(my_data[,1:ncol(my_data)])
#View(my_data[,100:ncol(my_data)])
str(my_data)

#'###Computing variables
#'####Computing mean workplace rank
my_data$WorkplaceMeanRank <- rowMeans(my_data[,c("Workplace_SR_Bin", "Workplace_US_IR_Bin")], na.rm = TRUE)

#'####Computing mean number of contributions per thread, avoiding division by zero
my_data$ContrPerThread <- my_data$PreviousContributions/(my_data$PreviousThreads + 0^my_data$PreviousThreads)

#'###Rescaling variables
#'Rescaling the Total_Citations and Word Count variables by two and three orders of magnitude, respectively. Now representing no. of citations and words in thousands and hundreds units, respectively.
#'Rescaling Unique Female Participation by a factor of 10. Now representing 10% units.
my_data$Total_Citations <- my_data$Total_Citations/1000
my_data$WC <- my_data$WC/100
my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation <- my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation * 10

#'###Defining measurement levels
#'####Defining variables as ordered or unordered factors
my_data$Female <- as.factor(my_data$Female)
my_data$Id_num <- as.factor(my_data$Id_num)
my_data$ThreadId <- as.factor(my_data$ThreadId)
my_data$WorkplaceMeanRank <- ordered(my_data$WorkplaceMeanRank)
my_data$AcademicHierarchyStrict <- ordered(my_data$AcademicHierarchyStrict)

#'####Some my_data checking
with(my_data, cor(UniqueContributors, UniqueMaleContributors + UniqueFemaleContributors))
with(my_data, cor(UniqueFemaleParticipation, UniqueFemaleContributors/UniqueContributors))
#UniqueContribution != UniqueMaleContributors + UniqueFemaleContributors (there must be some error in my_data generation)

#'###Descriptives
dat.subj.level <- my_data[!duplicated(my_data$Id_num),]

lapply(dat.subj.level[,c("Female", "Total_Citations", "WorkplaceMeanRank", 
                         "AcademicHierarchyStrict")],
       function(x){summary(x)})

#'###Plots
hist(my_data$WC[my_data$DebateSize > 1], xlab = "Word Count", breaks = 100)
hist(my_data$ContributionsbyAuthor[my_data$Female==1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1], xlab = "Contributions by Author")
table(my_data$ContributionsbyAuthor[my_data$Female==1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1])

#'##Hypothesis testing
#'###Hypothesis 1
#'**A womanâs tendency to participate actively in the conversation correlates positively with the number of females in the discussion.**

#'Random intercepts-only model for subject and thread
H1glmm0 <- glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ 1 + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId),
                 my_data, subset = (my_data$Female == 1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1), family="poisson", nAGQ = 1)

#'Model summary for H1glmm0
summary(H1glmm0)

#'Adding covariate - fixed effect of Contributions per Thread
H1glmm1 <- glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ 1 + ContrPerThread + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId),
                 my_data, subset = (my_data$Female == 1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1), family="poisson", nAGQ = 1)

#'Model summary, model comparison for H1glmm1
summary(H1glmm1)
anova(H1glmm0, H1glmm1)

#'Adding the target predictor - Unique Female Participation
H1glmm2 <- glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ 1 + ContrPerThread + UniqueFemaleParticipation + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId),
                 my_data, subset = (my_data$Female == 1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1), family="poisson", nAGQ = 1)

#'Model summary, model comparison, confidence intervals, R^2 for H1glmm2
summary(H1glmm2)
confint(H1glmm2)
anova(H1glmm1, H1glmm2)
rsquared(H1glmm2)

#'Computing Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF10), represented by the addition of the Unique Female Participation.
bf.approx <- 1/(exp((BIC(H1glmm2) - BIC(H1glmm1))/2))

#'Computing posterior probability of the parameter given 1:1 prior odds for H0:Ha
posterior <- bf.approx/(1+bf.approx)

#'Adding random slope for Unique Female Participation. Effect of unique female participation on Contributions by author now allowed to vary accross subjects.
H1glmm3 <- glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ 1 + ContrPerThread + UniqueFemaleParticipation + (1 + UniqueFemaleParticipation | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId),
                 my_data, subset = (my_data$Female == 1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1), family="poisson", nAGQ = 1)

#'Model summary, model comparison, confidence intervals, R^2 for H1glmm3
##reviewer 2 COMMENT I think H1glmm3 is the model analyst has used for  final report of efffect sizes
summary(H1glmm3)
anova(H1glmm2, H1glmm3)
confint(H1glmm3, parm = c("ContrPerThread", "UniqueFemaleParticipation"))
rsquared(H1glmm3)

#'Comparison model (having identical random effects structure)
H1glmm3a <- glmer(ContributionsbyAuthor ~ 1 + ContrPerThread + (1 + UniqueFemaleParticipation | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId),
                 my_data, subset = (my_data$Female == 1 & my_data$DebateSize > 1), family="poisson", nAGQ = 0)
anova(H1glmm3a, update(H1glmm3, nAGQ = 0))

#'Computing Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF10), represented by the addition of the Unique Female Participation, given the presence of the random slope.
bf.approx <- 1/(exp((BIC(H1glmm3) - BIC(H1glmm3a))/2))

#'Computing posterior probability of the parameter given 1:1 prior odds for H0:Ha
posterior <- bf.approx/(1+bf.approx)

#Plotting residuals against fitted values
plot(fitted(H1glmm3), residuals(H1glmm3), xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
lines(smooth.spline(fitted(H1glmm3), residuals(H1glmm3)))

#'###Hypothesis 2
#'**Higher status participants are more verbose than are lower status participants.**

#'Checking whether academics with missing Total_Citations differ in Word Count for conversations.
my_data$del <- is.na(my_data$Total_Citations)
t.test(WC ~ del, my_data, subset = my_data$DebateSize > 1 & my_data$Academic == 1)

#'Handling missing values by listwise deletion + filtering out non-conversations (single-authored threads)
#'Model comparison requires the exact same subset of my_data
nrow(my_data[my_data$DebateSize > 1 & !is.na(my_data$Total_Citations) & my_data$DebateSize > 1,])
table(with(my_data, complete.cases(AcademicHierarchyStrict, WorkplaceMeanRank, Total_Citations)))
data.na.rm = my_data[!is.na(my_data$AcademicHierarchyStrict) & !is.na(my_data$WorkplaceMeanRank) & !is.na(my_data$Total_Citations) & my_data$DebateSize > 1,]

#'Random intercepts-only model for subject and thread
H2lmm0 <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = TRUE)

#'Model summary for H2lmm0
summary(H2lmm0)

#'Adding Academic Hierarchy Strict as a blocking factor
H2lmm1 <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + AcademicHierarchyStrict + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = TRUE)

#'Model summary, model comparison for H2lmm1
summary(H2lmm1)
anova(H2lmm0, H2lmm1)

#'Adding Workplace Mean Rank as another blocking factor
H2lmm2 <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + WorkplaceMeanRank + AcademicHierarchyStrict + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = TRUE)

#'Model summary, model comparison for H2lmm2
summary(H2lmm2)
anova(H2lmm1, H2lmm2)

#'Adding the target predictor - Total Citations
H2lmm3 <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + WorkplaceMeanRank + AcademicHierarchyStrict + Total_Citations + (1 | Id_num) + (1 | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = TRUE)

#'Model summary, model comparison, confidence intervals, R^2 for H2lmm3
summary(H2lmm3)
anova(H2lmm2, H2lmm3)
confint(H2lmm3, parm = c("(Intercept)", "Total_Citations"))
rsquared(H2lmm3)

#'Computing Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF10), represented by the addition of Total Citations.
bf.approx <- 1/(exp((BIC(H2lmm3) - BIC(H2lmm2))/2))

#'Computing posterior probability of the parameter given 1:1 prior odds for H0:Ha
posterior <- bf.approx/(1+bf.approx)

#'Adding random slope for Total Citations. Effect of Total Citations on Word Count now allowed to vary accross threads
H2lmm4 <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + WorkplaceMeanRank + AcademicHierarchyStrict + Total_Citations + (1 | Id_num) + (1 + Total_Citations | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = TRUE)

#'Model summary, model comparison, confidence intervals (type = Wald), R^2 for H1glmm3
##reviewer 2 COMMENT: I think H2lmm4 is the model analyst used for reporting final effect sizes. Check variable "Total_Citations"
summary(H2lmm4)
anova(H2lmm3, H2lmm4)


confint(H2lmm4, parm = c("(Intercept)", "Total_Citations"), method = "Wald")
rsquared(H2lmm4)

#'Computing Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF10), represented by the addition of the random slope for Total Citations.
bf.approx <- 1/(exp((BIC(H2lmm4) - BIC(H2lmm3))/2))

#'Computing posterior probability of the parameter given 1:1 prior odds for H0:Ha
posterior <- bf.approx/(1+bf.approx)

#'Comparison model (having identical random effects structure)
H2lmm4a <- lmer(WC ~ 1 + WorkplaceMeanRank + AcademicHierarchyStrict  + (1 | Id_num) + (1 + Total_Citations | ThreadId), data.na.rm, REML = FALSE)
anova(H2lmm4a, update(H2lmm4, REML = FALSE))

#'Computing Bayes Factor in favor of the alternative hypothesis (BF10), represented by the addition of the fixed effect for Total Citations, given the presence of the random slope.
bf.approx <- 1/(exp((BIC(update(H2lmm4, REML = FALSE)) - BIC(H2lmm4a))/2))

#'Computing posterior probability of the parameter given 1:1 prior odds for H0:Ha
posterior <- bf.approx/(1+bf.approx)

#'Plotting residuals against fitted values
plot(fitted(H2lmm4), residuals(H2lmm4), xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
lines(smooth.spline(fitted(H2lmm4), residuals(H2lmm4)))

#'###Outliers detection
#'influence() uses brute iterative model estimation, it takes a few hours.

#'For model H1glmm3
#outliersH1glmm3 <- influence(update(H1glmm3, nAGQ = 0), obs = TRUE)
```

-Analyst 6
```{r}
#Hypothesis 2:
#Higher status participants are more verbose than are lower status participants.
# --------------------------------
rm(list = ls())
library(tidyverse)
#install.packages("GGally")
library(GGally)
library(car)
# --------------------------------
#Load data.
my_data <-read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")
# --------------------------------
#For each participant, calculate mean number of words per comment. --------
#First, calculate number of words in each comment. 
word_counts <- my_data %>% 
  dplyr::select(Title, Id, Text) %>%
  mutate(nwords = vapply(strsplit(Text, "\\W+"), length, integer(1)))
# --------------------------------
mean_wpc <- word_counts %>%
  group_by(Id) %>%
  summarise(mean_words = mean(nwords))
# --------------------------------
#Identify relevant status metrics. ----------
#First, get all potentially relevant metrics. 
status <- my_data %>% 
  filter(Limited_Information == 0) %>%
  dplyr::select(Title, Id, Role, Female, Male, Academic, Discipline,
                HavePhD, Years_from_PhD, PhD_Institution_SR_Bin, Workplace_SR_Bin,
                PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin, Workplace_US_IR_Bin, Total_Citations, H_Index, i10_Index,
                Citations_Year, Citations_Cumulative, AcademicHierarchyStrict)
#Make a correlation matrix to identify predictors. 
status %>%
  dplyr::select(-Title, -Id, -Role, -Female) %>%
  ggcorr
# --------------------------------
#Select a subset of predictors to reduce collinearity.
status <- status %>%
  dplyr::select(Title, Id, 
                H_Index, 
                AcademicHierarchyStrict,
                Workplace_US_IR_Bin,
                PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin,
                HavePhD)
status %>% select(-Title, -Id) %>% ggpairs()
#These correlations are all under ~0.6; will proceed with them. 
# --------------------------------
#Join status data with mean words per comment for each person. 
reg_dat <- left_join(mean_wpc, status, by = c("Id"))
# --------------------------------
#Regress mean number of words per comment against status metrics for that participant.-------
reg_dat <- reg_dat %>% select(-Title, -Id)
# --------------------------------
fit1 <- lm(mean_words ~ ., data = reg_dat)
summary(fit1)
vif(fit1)
plot(fit1)
alias(fit1)
# --------------------------------
#issues: 2119 is an outlier; aliased coefficients in model. 
#Aliased coefficients seem to be because many status measures depend on having a Phd.
#Solution: restrict analysis to people with PhDs (?)
# -------------------------------- 
#other ideas: maybe should be total words from that person per thread, rather than words per comment?
#redo word count as words per thread:
wpt_dat <- my_data %>%
  group_by(ThreadId, Id) %>%
  summarise(total_wpt = sum(WC)) %>%
  group_by(Id) %>%
  summarise(mean_wpt = sum(total_wpt)/n())
# --------------------------------
reg_dat <- left_join(wpt_dat, status, by = "Id") %>%
  group_by(Id) %>%
  slice(1)
reg_dat <- reg_dat %>% ungroup() %>% select(-Title, -Id)
# --------------------------------
#I'm considering leaving out the "have PhD category" - so first let's see whether it makes a difference on its own.
fit2 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ HavePhD, data = reg_dat)
summary(fit2)
# --------------------------------
#So people with PhDs are more verbose... with an extra 567 words per thread from PhDs. 
#Try subsetting to the group with PhDs anyway:
phds <- reg_dat %>% filter(HavePhD == 1) %>% select(-HavePhD)
fit3 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ ., data = phds)
summary(fit3)
vif(fit3)
plot(fit3)
# --------------------------------
#VIF looks okay. Point 155 definitely needs to go, though!
phds1 <- phds[-155,]
fit4 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ ., data = phds1)
summary(fit4)
plot(fit4)
sapply(phds1, function(x){sum(!is.na(x))})
nrow(complete.cases(phds1))
vif(fit4)
# --------------------------------
#H index is the only significant variable. Try just a regression against H index. 
fit5 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ H_Index, data = phds1)
summary(fit5)
# --------------------------------
#Wow, H-index by itself is not at all predictive. It's only predictive when controlling for other academic status metrics - so tempting to say that status isn't important? 
# --------------------------------
#What if we regress against another status metric by itself?
fit6 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ AcademicHierarchyStrict, data = phds1)
summary(fit6)
confint(fit6, 'AcademicHierarchyStrict', level = 0.95)
# --------------------------------
#That confirms earlier results; that academic hierarchy is not a good predictor. 
#Check other individual variables.
fit7 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ Workplace_US_IR_Bin, data = phds1)
summary(fit7)
# --------------------------------
#Same finding; check PhD institution:
fit8 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin, data = phds1)
summary(fit8)
# --------------------------------
#That also confirms that finding. 
#So, overall, a PhD does affect verbosity, but status doesn't seem to.
# --------------------------------
#check with interaction terms:
fit9 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin*H_Index,
           PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin*AcademicHierarchyStrict,
           PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin*Workplace_US_IR_Bin,
           AcademicHierarchyStrict*Workplace_US_IR_Bin,
           AcademicHierarchyStrict*H_Index,
           Workplace_US_IR_Bin*H_Index, data = phds1)
# --------------------------------
#one last idea: what if we just keep academics? this could include grad students. 
academics <- reg_dat %>%
  left_join(my_data) %>%
  filter(Academic == 1)
academics <- academics[,c("Id", "mean_wpt", names(status))]
academics <- academics %>%
  group_by(Id) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  select(-Id)
# --------------------------------
academics <- academics %>% select(-Title)
# --------------------------------
fit9 <- lm(mean_wpt ~ ., data = academics)
summary(fit9)
vif(fit9)
alias(fit9)
#This makes for the same problem as when all were included; aliasing included.
```

```{r}
my_data <- read.csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

### Hypothesis no 2 ###
# --------------------------------
# Model number of characters in contributions
# based on a couple of metrics for academic
# status
# --------------------------------
my_data <- my_data %>%
  mutate(log_cit = log10(Citations_Cumulative),
         log_char = log10(Number.Characters)) 
# --------------------------------
my_data %>%
  select(AcademicHierarchyStrict, Citations_Cumulative, 
         Number.Characters, log_cit, log_char) %>%

  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5) + 
  scale_y_log10() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_grid(Discipline ~ .) +
  theme_minimal()

  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5) +

  geom_smooth() +
  facet_grid(Discipline ~ .) +
  theme_minimal()
# --------------------------------

           Citations_Cumulative*Discipline, data = my_data)
summary(m3)
```

```{r}
my_data <- read_csv("C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv")

# Hyp. 2: “Higher status participants are more verbose than are lower status participants.”
# Status is tricky to operationalize. Let's define it by a linear combination of various
# variable obtained by factor analysis
# --------------------------------
# Building up the 'status' variable
z. <- function(X){
  (X - mean(X, na.rm=T))/sd(X, na.rm=T)
}
ind <- my_data$Id
# --------------------------------
phd <- my_data$HavePhD
phd[is.na(phd)] <- 0 # Assumes no info equals no PhD
phd <- tapply(phd, ind, mean)
# --------------------------------
academic <- as.numeric(my_data$Academic)
academic[is.na(academic)] <- 0 # Assumes no info equals not academic
academic <- tapply(academic, ind, mean)
# --------------------------------
phdBin <- my_data$PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin
phdBin[is.na(phdBin)] <- 0
phdBin <- tapply(phdBin, ind, mean)
phdBin <- z.(phdBin)
# --------------------------------
workBin <- my_data$Workplace_US_IR_Bin
workBin[is.na(workBin)] <- 0
workBin <- tapply(workBin, ind, mean)
workBin <- z.(workBin)
# --------------------------------
threadPart <- tapply(my_data$ThreadId, my_data$Id_num, function(x) length(unique(x))) # How many threads in total?
threadPart <- z.(threadPart)
# --------------------------------
# Citation indexes correlates highly with total citations
citation <- my_data$Total_Citations
citation[is.na(citation)] <- 0 # Assumes no info equals no citations
citation <- tapply(citation, ind, mean)
citation <- z.(citation)
# --------------------------------
acadHier <- my_data$AcademicHierarchyStrict
acadHier[is.na(acadHier)] <-0 # Again
acadHier <- tapply(acadHier, ind, mean)
acadHier <- z.(acadHier)
# --------------------------------
statusVar <- data.frame(phd, academic, phdBin, workBin, threadPart, citation, acadHier)
# --------------------------------
library(psych)
# --------------------------------
scree(na.exclude(statusVar)) # Seems like one factor is OK, even though it might not be theretically justifiable.
# 'loadings' weights come from factor analysis
loadings <- as.numeric(factanal(statusVar, factors=1)$loadings)
status <- apply(statusVar, 1, function(x) sum(x * loadings)/length(loadings))
status <- status[as.numeric(factor(my_data$Id))]
hist(status) # Seems to be bimodal, should we divide it?
# --------------------------------
hyp2df <- data.frame(Id=my_data$Id, ThreadId=my_data$ThreadId,
                     Role=my_data$Role, Female=my_data$Female,
                     WC=my_data$WC, Type=my_data$Type, status)
library(lme4)
# Use standardized status for easier interpratation
# Use 'factor' for easier to read summary
M1 <- (lmer(log(WC)~factor(Role) + factor(Female) + factor(Type) + z.(status) + (1|ThreadId) + (1|Id), data=hyp2df))
# --------------------------------
#Should we use a polynomial effect on status?
M2 <- (lmer(log(WC)~factor(Role) + factor(Female) + factor(Type) + poly(status, 2, raw=T) + (1|ThreadId) + (1|Id), data=hyp2df))
anova(M1, M2)
# Maybe we should, but we will ignore it for now.
# --------------------------------
# Residuals are not that great, but are reasonably centered at zero with some bad behavior in the extremes
plot(M1)
# But no significant correlation with the status variable
plot( status[!(is.na(my_data$Female))],predict(M1))
summary(M1) 
# For each standard-deviation in status, the word count increases around 13%.
```

```{r}
library('readr')

library('dplyr')

# Need to define verbosity: we use WPS
# Need to define status: 
# for non-academics; not a lot of information, but can use job titles.
# for academics: more information; use job hierarchy, citations, h-index
# also include: years from PhD, sex

# Load in data
my_data = read_csv('C:/ELTE_ST/Additional_research_activity/gamedev/Schweinsberg/data/edge1.1.csv')

# Filter out people with many contributions (Edge staff)
reduced.data = group_by(my_data, Id) %>% 
  summarize(Contribs=n()) %>%
  filter(Contribs < 100)
            
status.table = inner_join(reduced.data, my_data)  %>%
  select(WPS, Id, Live, Female, Academic, Job_Title_S, Years_from_PhD, 
         Total_Citations, H_Index, AcademicHierarchyStrict) %>%
  mutate(Log.Citations=log(Total_Citations))
?inner_join
# Scale continuous variables
status.table$WPS = scale(status.table$WPS)
status.table$Years_from_PhD = scale(status.table$Years_from_PhD)
status.table$Log.Citations = scale(status.table$Log.Citations)
status.table$H_Index = scale(status.table$H_Index)

?scale
# Need to treat academics and non-academics differently.
status.academic = filter(status.table, Academic==1) %>% 
  select(-Job_Title_S, -Academic)
status.nonacademic = filter(status.table, Academic==0) %>% 
  select(WPS, Id, Live, Female, Job_Title_S, Years_from_PhD) %>%
  filter(!grepl('Professor|Tenure|Academic', Job_Title_S))

# Analysis for academics

# Fit a random effects model with Gaussian link function
acad.model = lmer(WPS ~ Female + Years_from_PhD + Log.Citations + H_Index + AcademicHierarchyStrict + (1|Live),
                    data=status.academic)

summary(acad.model) ##reviewer 2 COMMENT: I think this is the model used by analyst in final report of effect size

# Analysis for non-academics

# Fit a random effects model with Gaussian link function
nonacad.model = lmer(WPS ~ Female + Years_from_PhD + Job_Title_S + (1|Live),
                    data=status.nonacademic)

summary(nonacad.model)
```

```{r}
# --------------------------------
Conversations<-filter(my_data, Type == 2, Live == 1, UniqueContributors > 1)
Ids<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Conversations$Id_num)))
Convs<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Conversations$ThreadId)))
# --------------------------------
# Academe<-filter(Conversations, Academic == 1)
# Non_Academe<-filter(Conversations, Academic == 0)

# Academe_Ids<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Academe$Id_num)))

# --------------------------------

#Non_Academe_Convs<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Non_Academe$ThreadId)))
# --------------------------------
#################################################################################################
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
Person_x_thread_Data<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,0,22))
# --------------------------------
for (i in 1:length(Ids)){
  Person  <- Ids[i]
  Convos<-filter(Conversations, Id_num ==  Person )
  Threads<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Convos$ThreadId)))
  for (j in 1:length(Threads)){
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,1,22))########
    # --------------------------------
    conv<-filter(Conversations, ThreadId ==  Threads[j] )
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,1]<-Person  # Id
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,2]<-Threads[j] #Thread Id
    conv_Person<-filter(conv, Id_num == Person)
    if(conv_Person$Order[1] == 1){Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,3]<-1} #Were they the lead? 
    # --------------------------------
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,4]<-dim(conv_Person)[1]/dim(conv)[1] #Fraction of total comments this person made
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,5]<-sum(conv_Person$Number.Characters) / sum(conv$Number.Characters) #Fraction of total characters from this person
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,6]<-conv_Person$Year[1] #Year
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,7]<-length(as.numeric(row.names(table(conv$Id_num)))) #Total number of people in the conversation
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,8]<-dim(conv)[1] #Total number of comments made
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,9]<-conv_Person$Female[1] #Female

Person_x_thread_Data<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,0,22))
# --------------------------------
for (i in 1:length(Ids)){
  Person  <- Ids[i]
  Convos<-filter(Online_Conversations, Id_num ==  Person )
  Threads<-as.numeric(row.names(table(Convos$ThreadId)))
  for (j in 1:length(Threads)){
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,1,22))########
    # --------------------------------
    conv<-filter(Online_Conversations, ThreadId ==  Threads[j] )
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,1]<-Person  # Id
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,2]<-Threads[j] #Thread Id
    conv_Person<-filter(conv, Id_num == Person)
    if(conv_Person$Order[1] == 1){Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,3]<-1} #Were they the lead? 
    # --------------------------------
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,4]<-dim(conv_Person)[1]/dim(conv)[1] #Fraction of total comments this person made
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,5]<-sum(conv_Person$Number.Characters) / sum(conv$Number.Characters) #Fraction of total characters from this person
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,6]<-conv_Person$Year[1] #Year
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,7]<-length(as.numeric(row.names(table(conv$Id_num)))) #Total number of people in the conversation
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,8]<-dim(conv)[1] #Total number of comments made
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,9]<-conv_Person$Female[1] #Female
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,10]<-conv_Person$Academic[1] #Academic
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,11]<-conv_Person$HavePhD[1] #HavePhD
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,12]<-conv_Person$PhD_Year[1] #PhD_Year 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,13]<-conv_Person$PhD_Institution_SR_Bin [1] #PhD Inst SR 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,14]<-conv_Person$Workplace_SR_Bin[1] #PhD Work SR 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,15]<-conv_Person$PhD_Institution_US_IR_Bin[1] #PhD Inst US 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,16]<-conv_Person$Workplace_US_IR_Bin[1] #PhD Work US 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,17]<-conv_Person$Total_Citations[1] #Total_Citations 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,18]<-conv_Person$H_Index[1] #H_Index
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,19]<-conv_Person$i10_Index[1] #i10_index
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,20]<-conv_Person$AcademicHierarchyStrict[1] #AcademicHierarchyStrict 
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,21]<-conv_Person$PreviousCitations[1] #PreviousCitations  
    Person_x_thread_Data_temp[1,22]<-conv_Person$Limited_Information[1] #PreviousCitations 
    # --------------------------------
    Person_x_thread_Data<-rbind(Person_x_thread_Data,Person_x_thread_Data_temp)
    # --------------------------------
  }
  # --------------------------------
  # --------------------------------
  # --------------------------------
  # --------------------------------
}
```

```{r}
# After loading the data, we are going to investigate a bit the different variables so that we can
# have an idea about how the data look like. This is important to do before
# moving to the main analyses as we may have to do also a lot of cleaning
# before the main analyses -- e.g., a lot of NAs or weird variables.
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Year) %>% table %>% barplot(ylim = c(150, 1500), xpd = FALSE, las = 0)
# From the barplot we see that there is variability in the number of lines per year.
# This could be for different reasons that will be probably be explained later as we explore
# the data set. 
# --------------------------------
# Now we are going to check what type of conversations we have, and how those conversations are
# distributed per year
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Year, Type) %>% table()
# Apart from years 1996, and 1997 there seems to be more contributions in converstations than
# the annual questions. This makes sense of course.
# --------------------------------
# Now, what could be interesting is to see how much unique are these questions
# UNCOMMENT TO RUN my_data %>% dplyr::select(Title, Year, Type) %>% table
# OK, that is a bit too long to read and not informative enough
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# OK, maybe things get a bit interesting now. We are going to run the
# descriptive for male and female contributions
layout(1:2)
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Male_Contributions)   %>% table %>% barplot(main = "male")
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Female_Contributions) %>% table %>% barplot(main = "female")
# So, if I am understanding this right, men speak much more than women. There
# is a problem with the y axis, but still, this is what it looks like. I will
# also run frequenceis just to see the raw numbers
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Male_Contributions)   %>% table()
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Female_Contributions) %>% table()
# ... and the sums
attr(table(dplyr::select(my_data, Male_Contributions)), "dimnames")[[1]] %>% as.numeric() %>% sum()
attr(table(dplyr::select(my_data, Female_Contributions)), "dimnames")[[1]] %>% as.numeric() %>% sum()
# OK, huge differences here. Preliminary but still a first look on this variables
# --------------------------------
# Seeing female participation

# These are way too low percentages

my_data %>% dplyr::select(NumberofAuthorContributions) %>% table %>% barplot
# OK good. Maybe this is a bit wrong analysis because there are many zeros (this
# refers to the annual questions). So, once again without the zeros
my_data %>% dplyr::select(NumberofAuthorContributions) %>% dplyr::filter(NumberofAuthorContributions > 0) %>%table() %>% barplot()
#OK good.
# Debate Size
my_data %>% dplyr::select(DebateSize) %>% table() %>% barplot()
# So, many conversations have large sizes from what I can see
# --------------------------------
# Descriptives of unique contributors
my_data %>% dplyr::select(UniqueContributors)        %>% table()  %>% barplot (main = "Unique Contributors")

# Super low percentages
# --------------------------------
# We skip some variables and we do descriptives for males and females
# Here we do piecharts just because some people hate them
layout(t(1:2))
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Male)   %>% table() %>% pie (main = "Male")
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Female) %>% table() %>% pie (main = "Female")
# --------------------------------
# Job titles
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Job_Title_S) %>% table()
# BTW, we do not have data for 254 participants. Most participants are professors (2442)
# --------------------------------
# Contributions this year
my_data %>% dplyr::select(ContributionsThisYear) %>% table()
# Most people participate 1s.
my_data %>% dplyr::select(ThreadsThisYear) %>% table()
# Again, once is the main number
# --------------------------------
# PhD Institution US IR 
my_data %>% dplyr::select(PhD_Institution_US_IR) %>% table()
# Most people come from the 1st university?
# --------------------------------
# PhD Institution US 
my_data %>% dplyr::select(PhD_Institution_US) %>% table()
# Again 1st is the dominant
# --------------------------------
# H_Index 
my_data %>% dplyr::select(H_Index) %>% table() %>% barplot()
# Most people are around 50 index
# --------------------------------
# i10_index 
my_data %>% dplyr::select(i10_Index) %>% table() %>% barplot()
# It is around 70
# --------------------------------
# Citations_Cumulative 
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Citations_Cumulative) %>% table() %>% barplot()
# Around 5000 publications
# --------------------------------
# Number_Characters
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Number.Characters) %>% table() %>% barplot()
my_data %>% dplyr::select(Number.Characters) %>% describe()
# --------------------------------
# This is the very basic hypothesis testing. This is done out
# of curioucity at this stage as there are many other variables that you need
# to control with.
# First plots
plot(density(my_data$Female_Contributions))
# OK, this shows really skewed distributions
plot(density(my_data$UniqueFemaleContributors))
# Also this one
# --------------------------------
# Now a bit more formal test
ks.test(my_data$Female_Contributions, "pnorm")
ks.test(my_data$UniqueFemaleContributors, "pnorm")
# OK, this is useful. There are ties in the data. As such
# it would be problematic to use parametric tests. Of course
# the KS also shows that the distributions are not normal but maybe
# a significant result is normal given the amount of data.
# --------------------------------
# Since we have ties, and the assumption of normality is violated,
# it makes most sense to run kendal's tau for the correlation. But first,
# let's make a scatterplot with the data
plot(x = my_data$Female_Contributions,  y = my_data$UniqueFemaleContributors)
# OK, this is so interesting. There seems to be two separate lines.
# This is probably due to the many zeros. Yes, the variables are problematic
# as, as also shown in the barplots above, many women just do not participate.
# OK, so let's remove the zeros
dtmp <- my_data %>% dplyr::select(Female_Contributions, UniqueFemaleContributors) #%>% 
dtmp <- dtmp[dtmp$Female_Contributions != 0 & dtmp$UniqueFemaleContributors != 0, ]
plot(x = dtmp$Female_Contributions,  y = dtmp$UniqueFemaleContributors)
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
#dtmp$Female_Contributions %>% table
#cor.test
#cor.test(my_data$Female_Contributions, my_data$UniqueFemaleContributors)
#lm(my_data$Female_Contributions~my_data$UniqueFemaleContributors) %>% summary
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# OK, here we explore two other relevant variables, namely the UniqueFemaleContributors and
# FemaleParticipation
plot(x = my_data$FemaleParticipation,  y = my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation)
plot(x = my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = my_data$FemaleParticipation)
# OK, here there seems to be a relationship between variables but we
# have plenty of outliers that have an effect. I think we should do something
# about it.
# One option is to remove the outliers, especially the ones at 1. But
# I am a bit against that unless absolutely necessary. A common approach
# in dealing with outliers is to actually use robust methods. I am all
# for Bayesian but first let's see what we can do with the frequentist's approach.
corKendall(x = my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = my_data$FemaleParticipation, consistent = TRUE)
corKendall(x = my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = my_data$FemaleParticipation, consistent = FALSE)
# OK, both tests, show a positive correlation. Please note that we use Kendall test 
# because we have ties in our data. 
# --------------------------------
# Maybe check how the results could change if we remove the very extreme outliers
my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation %>% describe
my_data$FemaleParticipation       %>% describe
#
my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation [which(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation > mean(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation) + 3*sd(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation))]
# --------------------------------
my_data$FemaleParticipation [which(my_data$FemaleParticipation > mean(my_data$FemaleParticipation) + 3*sd(my_data$FemaleParticipation))]
# --------------------------------
my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation [which(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation < mean(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation) - 3*sd(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation))]
# --------------------------------
my_data$FemaleParticipation [which(my_data$FemaleParticipation < mean(my_data$FemaleParticipation) - 3*sd(my_data$FemaleParticipation))]
# --------------------------------
# OK, we have to remove a lot of values (for the positive limit actually). We do that for exploratory reasons.
# --------------------------------
d1 <- my_data[-which(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation > (mean(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation) + (3*sd(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation)))), ]
d1 <- d1[-which(d1$FemaleParticipation > (mean(d1$FemaleParticipation) + (3*sd(d1$FemaleParticipation)))), ]
# Plot the data
plot(x = d1$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = d1$FemaleParticipation)
# OK, the data look a bit better now. Now, let's run again the robust Kendall
corKendall(x = d1$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = d1$FemaleParticipation, consistent = TRUE)
corKendall(x = d1$UniqueFemaleParticipation,  y = d1$FemaleParticipation, consistent = FALSE)
# Again, we see a positive correlation.
# --------------------------------
# Now we are going to run a Bayesian Hypothesis Testing test. Please note we 001: use the original variables,
# without removing outliers. We used the Savage Dickey approach because the non-Savage Dickey approach
# had a problem with integarting with infinity.
# UNCOMMENT bcor <- jzs_corSD(V1 = my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation, V2 = my_data$FemaleParticipation, alternative = "greater")
# --------------------------------
# OK, so even the jzs_corSD did not work all of the times. When it worked it showed stong
# We will investigate if we get more 
# reliable results if we actually remove outliers
# --------------------------------
# OK, let's see what we can do with the code provided here:
# http://www.sumsar.net/blog/2013/08/robust-bayesian-estimation-of-correlation/
robust_model_string <- 
  model {
    for(i in 1:n) {
      # We've replaced dmnorm with and dmt ...
      x[i,1:2] ~ dmt(mu[], prec[ , ], nu) 
    }
# --------------------------------
    prec[1:2,1:2] <- inverse(cov[,])
    # --------------------------------
    cov[1,1] <- sigma[1] * sigma[1]
    cov[1,2] <- sigma[1] * sigma[2] * rho
    cov[2,1] <- sigma[1] * sigma[2] * rho
    cov[2,2] <- sigma[2] * sigma[2]
    # --------------------------------
    sigma[1] ~ dunif(0, 1000) 
    sigma[2] ~ dunif(0, 1000)
    rho ~ dunif(-1, 1)
    mu[1] ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
    mu[2] ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
    # --------------------------------
    # ... and added a prior on the degree of freedom parameter nu.
    nu <- nuMinusOne+1
    nuMinusOne ~ dexp(1/29)
    # --------------------------------
    x_rand ~ dmt(mu[], prec[ , ], nu)
  }

#################################################################################################
#################################################################################################
#####   This R-code serves to compute a Bayes factor for Kendall's tau, as described in     #####
#####   van Doorn, J.B., Ly, A., Marsman, M. & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (in press). Bayesian      #####
#####   Inference for Kendallâ€™s Rank Correlation Coefficient. The American Statistician.    #####
#################################################################################################
#####   To use it, input your values below for yourKendallTauValue and yourN and run the    #####
#####   whole script. The function call at the bottom will use your values and will compute #####
#####   and print the Bayes factor in the console. The last line will plot the posterior    #####
#####   distribution. This analysis is also available in JASP (www.jasp-stats.org), an      #####
#####   open-source statistical software for Bayesian statistics with a graphical user      #####
#####   interface.                                                               #####
#################################################################################################
#################################################################################################
# --------------------------------
yourKendallTauValue <- cor(my_data$UniqueFemaleParticipation, my_data$FemaleParticipation, method = "kendall")                      # Input your obtained value for kendall's 001: tau here
yourN <- 100                    # Input your sample size here, then run the whole script
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# Prior specification Kendall's Tau
scaledBetaTau <- function(tau, alpha=1, beta=1){
  result <-   ((pi*2^(-2*alpha))/beta(alpha,alpha))  * cos((pi*tau)/2)^(2*alpha-1)
  return(result)
}
# --------------------------------
priorTau <- function(tau, kappa){
  scaledBetaTau(tau, alpha = (1/kappa), beta = (1/kappa))
}
# --------------------------------
priorTauPlus <- function(tau, kappa=1) {
  non.negative.index <- tau >=0
  less.than.one.index <- tau <=1
  value.index <- as.logical(non.negative.index*less.than.one.index)
  result <- tau*0
  result[value.index] <- 2*priorTau(tau[value.index], kappa)
  return(result)
}
# --------------------------------
priorTauMin <- function(tau, kappa=1) {
  negative.index <- tau <=0
  greater.than.min.one.index <- tau >= -1
  value.index <- as.logical(negative.index*greater.than.min.one.index)
  result <- tau*0
  result[value.index] <- 2*priorTau(tau[value.index], kappa)
  return(result)
}
# --------------------------------
# Posterior specification Kendall's Tau
postDensKendallTau <- function(delta,Tstar,n,kappa=1,var=var,test="two-sided"){ 
  if(test == "two-sided"){priorDens <- priorTau(delta,kappa)
  } else if(test == "positive"){priorDens <- priorTauPlus(delta,kappa)
  } else if(test == "negative"){priorDens <- priorTauMin(delta,kappa)}
  priorDens <- priorTau(delta,kappa)
  dens <- dnorm(Tstar,(1.5*delta*sqrt(n)),sd=sqrt(var))* priorDens
  return(dens)
}
posteriorTau <- function(delta,kentau,n,kappa=1,var=1,test="two-sided"){
  Tstar <- (kentau * ((n*(n-1))/2))/sqrt(n*(n-1)*(2*n+5)/18)
  var <- min(1,var)
  if(test == "two-sided"){lims <- c(-1,1)
  } else if(test == "positive"){lims <- c(0,1)
  } else if(test == "negative"){lims <- c(-1,0)}
  logicalCensor <- (delta >= lims[1] & delta <= lims[2])
  dens <- logicalCensor*postDensKendallTau(delta,Tstar,n,kappa,var,test=test)/
    integrate(function(delta){postDensKendallTau(delta,Tstar,n,kappa,var,test=test)},lims[1],lims[2])$value
} 
# --------------------------------
# Bayes factor computation Kendall's Tau
bfCorrieKernelKendallTau <- function(tau, n, kappa=1, var=1, ciValue=0.95){ 
  tempList <- list(vector())
  output <- list(n=n, r=tau, bf10=NA, bfPlus0=NA, bfMin0=NA)
  output$bf10 <- priorTau(0,kappa)/posteriorTau(0,tau,n,kappa=kappa,var=var,test="two-sided")
  output$bfPlus0 <- priorTauPlus(0,kappa)/posteriorTau(0,tau,n,kappa=kappa,var=var,test="positive")
  output$bfMin0 <- priorTauMin(0,kappa)/posteriorTau(0,tau,n,kappa=kappa,var=var,test="negative")
  return(output)
}
# --------------------------------
# Compute credible intervals kendalls tau
credibleIntervalKendallTau <- function(kentau,n,kappa=1,var=1, test="two-sided", ciValue = 0.95){
  nSeqs <- 1000
  lowCI <- (1-ciValue)/2
  upCI <- (1+ciValue)/2
  taus <- seq(-1,1,length.out = (nSeqs-1))
  densVals <- posteriorTau(taus, kentau, n, kappa = kappa, var = var, test = test)
  densVals <- cumsum((densVals[1:(nSeqs-1)]+densVals[2:nSeqs])*0.5*(taus[2]-taus[1]))
  lowerCI <- taus[which(densVals>=lowCI)[1]]
  upperCI <- taus[which(densVals>=upCI)[1]]
  median <- taus[which(densVals>=0.5)[1]]
  return(list(lowerCI = lowerCI, median = median, upperCI = upperCI))
}
# --------------------------------
sampleTausA <- function(myTau,myN,nSamples = 3e3, var = 1){
  nSeqs <- 1000
  tauSamples <- NULL
  taus <- seq(-1,1,length.out = nSeqs)
  densVals <- posteriorTau(taus, myTau, myN, var = var)
  ceiling <- max(densVals)
  lowerB <- taus[which(round(densVals,digits=6) != 0 )][1]
  upperB <- rev(taus[which(round(densVals,digits=6) != 0 )])[1]
  # --------------------------------
  while(length(tauSamples) < nSamples){
    prop <- runif(1,lowerB,upperB)
    propDens <- posteriorTau(prop, myTau, myN, var = var)
    if(propDens > runif(1,0,ceiling)){tauSamples <- c(tauSamples,prop)}
  }
  return(tauSamples)
}
# --------------------------------
bfCorrieKernelKendallTau(tau = yourKendallTauValue, n = yourN)  # This function call will carry out the computations
# and returns a list with the Bayes factors (regular, plussided, minsided)
# --------------------------------
# The following code plots a (simple) posterior distribution of your results.
layout(1)
plot(density(sampleTausA(myTau = yourKendallTauValue, myN = yourN),from = -1, to = 1), las = 1, bty = "n", lwd=3, 
     main = "Posterior Distribution for Kendall's tau", xlab = expression(tau))
```

```{r}
# create variable for all contributions of a given person

      mutate(AllContributions = PreviousContributions + ContributionsThisYear)
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# calculate average comment length per commenter
dat_sum <- dat2 %>% 
            mutate(AllContributions = PreviousContributions + ContributionsThisYear) %>% 
            group_by(Id) %>% 
            # Academic Status might change, so taking the mean. This is not ideal though.
            summarise(AcademicHierarchyStrict = mean(AcademicHierarchyStrict),
                      comment_length = mean(Number.Characters),
                      number_comments = mean(AllContributions))
# --------------------------------
# check distribution of Academic Hierachy
dat_sum %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = AcademicHierarchyStrict)) + geom_histogram()
# --> groups are very unequal
# --------------------------------
# plot
dat_sum %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = AcademicHierarchyStrict, y = comment_length)) + 
  geom_point(aes(size = number_comments)) +
  geom_smooth()
# --------------------------------
# --------------------------------
# modeling: 1st model
hist(dat_sum$comment_length, breaks = 100)
hist(dat_sum$number_comments, breaks = 100)
hist(dat_sum$AcademicHierarchyStrict, breaks = 100)
# --------------------------------
# Don't take the mean of AcademicHierarchy 
dat_sum <- dat2 %>% 
  mutate(AllContributions = PreviousContributions + ContributionsThisYear) %>% 
  group_by(Id, AcademicHierarchyStrict, Female) %>% 
  # Academic Status might change, so taking the mean. This is not ideal though.
  summarise(
            comment_length = mean(Number.Characters),
            number_comments = mean(AllContributions))
# --------------------------------
# look at it by male vs female
dat_sum %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = AcademicHierarchyStrict, y = comment_length, 
             color = factor(Female))) + 
  geom_point(aes(size = number_comments)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = factor(Female)))
# --------------------------------
hist(dat_sum$AcademicHierarchyStrict, breaks = 100)
# --------------------------------
# we want academic hierarchy as a predictor.
# code ordinal variable as numeric, as Andrew Gelman suggests here: http://andrewgelman.com/2009/10/06/coding_ordinal/
dat_sum <- dat_sum %>% mutate(AH = as.numeric(as.character(AcademicHierarchyStrict)))
# --------------------------------
# simple linear model
# comment_length
mod1 <- lm(comment_length ~ AH + as.factor(Female), data = dat_sum)
summary(mod1) # -239.01   [-553.3450   75.33359] 
standardize_parameters(mod1)
library(lme4)
mod4 = lmer(comment_length ~ AH + as.factor(Female) + (1|Id), data = dat_sum)
summary(mod4)
lmerTest::as_lmerModLmerTest(mod4)
standardize_parameters(mod4)
# --------------------------------
# plot(mod1)
CI_mod1 <- confint(mod1)
# --------------------------------
# number of comments
# model number of comments too
mod2 <- lm(number_comments ~ AH + as.factor(Female), data = dat_sum)
summary(mod2) # 1.6627 [ -0.6519959  3.977397]
standardize_parameters(mod2)
# plot(mod2)
CI_mod2 <- confint(mod2)
CI_mod2
# --------------------------------
# within the university hierarchy there doesn't seem to be a trend, however, the lower level
# groups are less represented in the dataset.
```
